nameStory: The White Slant-line gets its name from the distinctive diagonal white lines that streak across its wings at an angle, creating a slanted pattern that's easy to spot. These slanted markings set it apart from moths with straight lines or curved patterns, making the name both descriptive and practical for identification.
description: The White Slant-line is a medium-sized moth in the geometer family, known for the characteristic way their caterpillars move by 'measuring' the earth with their bodies. Adults have forewings that span about three-quarters to one inch across, decorated with the telltale white diagonal lines that give them their name. Like other geometers, they have a delicate build and hold their wings horizontally when at rest, creating a triangular silhouette.

idTips.label: White diagonal lines
idTips.description: Look for distinct white slanted lines crossing the forewings at an angle - these are the moth's signature feature and feel smooth to the touch if you're examining a specimen

idTips.label: Wing position at rest
idTips.description: Wings are held horizontally outward from the body when resting, creating a flat triangular shape rather than the tent-like posture of many other moths

idTips.label: Size range
idTips.description: Forewings measure roughly 19-26mm long, making them noticeably smaller than your thumb but larger than your pinky nail

idTips.label: Body build
idTips.description: Has the typical slender, delicate build of geometer moths with a relatively thin body compared to the wingspan

idTips.label: Flight period timing
idTips.description: Adults are active from late spring through early summer, typically May through early July, when they're attracted to lights on warm evenings

habitat: White Slant-lines are found in mixed and deciduous forests throughout New England, particularly where their host trees grow abundantly. Look for them in areas with birches, willows, elms, and various conifers, as their caterpillars feed on this diverse range of trees. They're equally at home in lowland woods and higher elevation forests up into the mountains.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late May as temperatures warm, making this the start of the best viewing season. Look for them at porch lights and outdoor lighting during mild evenings.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs through June and into early July when adults are most abundant and actively mating. This is your best chance to spot them, especially on warm, humid nights.
seasonality.fall: Adults have finished their flight period, but look for small green caterpillars measuring their way along branches of host trees as they prepare for winter.
seasonality.winter: The species overwinters as pupae tucked away in leaf litter or soil, completely hidden from view until the next spring's emergence.

funFact: White Slant-line caterpillars are incredible botanical generalists, able to munch on everything from delicate birch leaves to tough conifer needles - a dietary flexibility that would be like a person thriving equally well on salad greens and tree bark!
confusionNotes: White Slant-lines can be confused with other small geometer moths that also have light-colored wing markings, but the specific diagonal white lines are the key distinguisher. Remember: if the white markings slant like a forward slash (/), you've likely found your White Slant-line.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'cachexiata' comes from a Greek word meaning 'wasted' or 'emaciated,' possibly referring to the moth's delicate, slender appearance typical of the geometer family. This family name 'Geometridae' literally means 'earth measurers' in reference to how the caterpillars loop their bodies to move forward.
compareHints: Since White Slant-line is the only Tetracis species in our dataset for New England, compare it with other small geometer moths in the region. Unlike many of its geometer cousins that have curved or wavy lines, the White Slant-line's markings are distinctly straight and diagonal. The combination of white slanted lines and medium size makes it fairly distinctive among New England's geometer moth community.
